Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds, and may Allah send blessings and peace upon our Prophet Muhammad, and upon his family and companions, and those who follow them in goodness until the Day of Judgment.

(...) We speak about the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿For the covenant of the Quraysh, their covenant of the journey of winter and summer. So let them worship the Lord of this House, who has fed them against hunger and made them safe from fear.﴾ [Quraysh 1–4].

This surah is connected to the surah before it, for the surah before it explains Allah's favour upon the people of Makkah by what He did to the companions of the elephant, who intended to come to Makkah to demolish the Ka'bah. Then Allah explains in this surah another great blessing upon the people of Makkah, upon the Quraysh: that they had two journeys in the year, one in summer and one in winter.

The word ilaf (الإيلاف) means gathering and joining together, and what is meant by it is the trade that they used to carry out, once in winter and once in summer. In winter they headed toward Yemen for its agricultural produce, and because its climate is suitable; and in summer they headed toward al-Sham (Greater Syria), because most of the trade in fruits and other goods takes place at this time, in summer, along with the suitability of the cool weather. So this is a blessing from Allah the Exalted upon the Quraysh in these two journeys. The first journey: the journey of winter — at what time?

* A student: Winter.

* The Shaykh: To which direction? Yemen. And the second: the journey of summer toward al-Sham.

When He reminded them of this blessing, which is a great blessing because many benefits and great gains result from this trade, the Mighty and Majestic commanded them to worship the Lord of this House; He said: ﴿So let them worship the Lord of this House﴾, in gratitude to Him for this blessing. This fa' (فاء) may either be the fa' of causation, meaning: because of these two journeys, let them worship the Lord of this House; or it may be the fa' of consequence (تفريع). Whichever it is, it is built upon what preceded; that is: because of these great blessings, it is obligatory upon them to worship Allah.

Worship (العبادة) is humbling oneself before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, out of love and glorification: that a person worships Allah, humbles himself to Him through hearing and obedience. When a command reaches him from Allah and His Messenger, he says: "We hear and we obey", and when a report reaches him he says: "We hear and we believe", out of love and glorification. By love a person carries out the commands, and by glorification he abandons the prohibitions out of fear of this Mighty One, the Mighty and Majestic. This is one meaning of worship.

The term worship is also applied to the thing that is worshipped itself, and Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, defined it in this sense, saying: "Worship is a comprehensive term for everything that Allah loves and is pleased with, of sayings and deeds, apparent and hidden." Hence, if someone asked you: "What is prayer? Is it worship or habit?", you would say: "Worship." And if someone asked you: "You are now praying, so what is the meaning of this prayer of yours?", you would say: "Its meaning is worship of Allah. I worship Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; I humble myself to Him through hearing and obedience and by what He has commanded me."

As for His saying: ﴿the Lord of this House﴾, it refers to the honoured Ka'bah, and Allah the Exalted has attributed it to Himself in His saying: ﴿And purify My House for those who circumambulate, stand, bow and prostrate﴾ [al-Hajj 26]. Here He attributed its lordship to Himself, saying: ﴿the Lord of this House﴾.

Is He the Lord of other things too? The answer: Yes, but the attribution of lordship to Him here is by way of honour and glorification.

Now, ﴿My House﴾ — is not everything Allah's? To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth; everything belongs to Allah, everything is Allah's possession. Why then did Allah attribute the House to Himself? For honour and glorification.

So He specified it with lordship, that is, He specified the House with lordship once, and attributed it to Himself another time, for honour and glorification.

In another verse: ﴿I have only been commanded to worship the Lord of this city, which He has made sacred﴾, and after it, what did He say? ﴿And to Him belongs everything﴾ [an-Naml 91], as a safeguard lest some deluded person imagine that He is the Lord of the city alone; so He said: ﴿And to Him belongs everything﴾. Each context has a fitting expression. In His saying: ﴿I have only been commanded to worship the Lord of this city, which He has made sacred﴾ there is a context requiring the explanation of the generality of His dominion, lest the polytheists claim that He is only the Lord of the city; but here the context is one of glorifying the House, so mentioning it alone was appropriate.

﴿Who has fed them against hunger and made them safe from fear﴾. ﴿Who﴾ (الذي): is this an adjective of ﴿Lord﴾ or of ﴿House﴾?

* Students: Of ﴿Lord﴾.

* The Shaykh: Of ﴿Lord﴾. So its position is in the accusative case (نصب), and for this reason it is good to pause and say: ﴿So let them worship the Lord of this House﴾, then say: ﴿who has fed them﴾; because if you connected and said: ﴿the Lord of this House (3) who has fed them﴾, the listener would think that ﴿who﴾ is an adjective of ﴿House﴾, and this is far from the meaning and the meaning would not stand.

﴿Who has fed them against hunger and made them safe from fear﴾: Allah the Exalted explained His blessing upon them, both the apparent and the hidden blessing. Feeding them against hunger is a protection from perishing in a hidden matter, which is the food they eat; and ﴿made them safe from fear﴾ is a protection from disagreement in the matter — what? — the apparent; because fear is apparent. When the lands are surrounded by enemies, their people fear and refrain from going out and remain in their shelters. So Allah reminded them of this blessing: ﴿He fed them against hunger and made them safe from fear﴾. The safest place on earth is Makkah; it is the safest place on earth, and therefore its trees are not cut, its grass is not uprooted, its fallen things are not picked up except by one who will announce them, its game is not hunted, and blood is not shed in it. These characteristics are not found in other lands. Even Madinah is sacred and has a sanctuary (haram), but its sanctuary is far below the sanctuary of Makkah. The sanctuary of Makkah: no Muslim can enter it who has not entered it for the first time except in ihram; he is obliged to enter in ihram. Madinah is not like that. The sanctuary of Makkah makes its grass and trees forbidden absolutely, whereas for the sanctuary of Madinah some of its trees are permitted for cultivation and the like. The game of Makkah is forbidden and there is a penalty for it; the game of Madinah carries no penalty. The main point is that the greatest safe place is Makkah; even the trees are safe in it, and even the game is safe in it. Were it not that Allah made things easy for His servants, even the livestock — I mean the cattle that are not game — would be... but Allah has had mercy on the servants and permitted them to slaughter and sacrifice in this place. This blessing Allah reminded them of in His saying: ﴿Have they not seen that We made a sacred sanctuary secure, while people are snatched away from around them?﴾ [al-'Ankabut 67]; meaning: will they not thank Allah for this? So this surah, as you see, is entirely a reminder to the Quraysh of what Allah has bestowed upon them in this great House, in security from fear, and in feeding from hunger.

If someone says: What is the duty of the Quraysh regarding this blessing? And likewise, what is the duty of whoever dwells in Makkah now, of the Quraysh or others?

We say: The duty is gratitude to Allah the Exalted by performing His obedience, carrying out His command and avoiding His prohibitions. For this reason, when sins increase in the sanctuary, the danger to its people is greater than the danger to others, because sin in a noble place is greater than sin in a less noble place. This is why Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And whoever intends therein deviation by wrongdoing — We will make him taste a painful punishment﴾ [al-Hajj 25]. Allah threatened whoever intends within it — that is, whoever resolves within it upon deviation — let alone one who actually commits deviation.

It is obligatory upon a person to remember Allah's blessing upon him in every place, not only in Makkah. Our country, praise be to Allah, is today among the safest countries of the world, and among the most abundant and comfortable of the world's countries in livelihood. Allah has fed us against hunger and made us safe from fear. So it is incumbent upon us to thank Allah for this blessing, to cooperate in righteousness and piety, in enjoining good and forbidding evil, in calling to Allah upon insight, with deliberation and carefulness, and to be brothers bound together in affection.

And it is obligatory upon us — especially upon students of knowledge — when they differ among themselves, to sit together for consultation and calm discussion aimed at reaching the truth. Whenever the truth becomes clear to a person, it is obligatory upon him to follow it, and it is not permissible for him to defend his opinion, because he is not an infallible lawgiver who says: "My opinion is the correct one and whatever else is wrong." The obligation upon the believing person is to be as Allah wants him to be: ﴿It is not for a believing man or a believing woman, when Allah and His Messenger have decreed a matter, that they should have any choice about their affair. And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger has certainly strayed into clear error﴾ [al-Ahzab 36]. As for a person defending his opinion and insisting upon what he is on even when it has become clear to him that it is false, this is an error; this is the habit of the polytheists who refused to follow the Messenger and said: ﴿Indeed, we found our fathers upon a religion, and indeed we are following in their footsteps, guided﴾ [az-Zukhruf 22].

We ask Allah to perpetuate for us and for you the blessing of Islam and security in our homelands, and to make us brothers bound together upon the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him and upon his family.

Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds, and may Allah send blessings and peace upon our Prophet Muhammad, and upon his family and companions, and those who follow them in goodness until the Day of Judgment.

(...) We speak about the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿For the covenant of the Quraysh, their covenant of the journey of winter and summer. So let them worship the Lord of this House, who has fed them against hunger and made them safe from fear.﴾ [Quraysh 1–4].

This surah is connected to the surah before it, for the surah before it explains Allah's favour upon the people of Makkah by what He did to the companions of the elephant, who intended to come to Makkah to demolish the Ka'bah. Then Allah explains in this surah another great blessing upon the people of Makkah, upon the Quraysh: that they had two journeys in the year, one in summer and one in winter.

The word ilaf (الإيلاف) means gathering and joining together, and what is meant by it is the trade that they used to carry out, once in winter and once in summer. In winter they headed toward Yemen for its agricultural produce, and because its climate is suitable; and in summer they headed toward al-Sham (Greater Syria), because most of the trade in fruits and other goods takes place at this time, in summer, along with the suitability of the cool weather. So this is a blessing from Allah the Exalted upon the Quraysh in these two journeys. The first journey: the journey of winter — at what time?

* A student: Winter.

* The Shaykh: To which direction? Yemen. And the second: the journey of summer toward al-Sham.

When He reminded them of this blessing, which is a great blessing because many benefits and great gains result from this trade, the Mighty and Majestic commanded them to worship the Lord of this House; He said: ﴿So let them worship the Lord of this House﴾, in gratitude to Him for this blessing. This fa' (فاء) may either be the fa' of causation, meaning: because of these two journeys, let them worship the Lord of this House; or it may be the fa' of consequence (تفريع). Whichever it is, it is built upon what preceded; that is: because of these great blessings, it is obligatory upon them to worship Allah.

Worship (العبادة) is humbling oneself before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, out of love and glorification: that a person worships Allah, humbles himself to Him through hearing and obedience. When a command reaches him from Allah and His Messenger, he says: "We hear and we obey", and when a report reaches him he says: "We hear and we believe", out of love and glorification. By love a person carries out the commands, and by glorification he abandons the prohibitions out of fear of this Mighty One, the Mighty and Majestic. This is one meaning of worship.

The term worship is also applied to the thing that is worshipped itself, and Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, defined it in this sense, saying: "Worship is a comprehensive term for everything that Allah loves and is pleased with, of sayings and deeds, apparent and hidden." Hence, if someone asked you: "What is prayer? Is it worship or habit?", you would say: "Worship." And if someone asked you: "You are now praying, so what is the meaning of this prayer of yours?", you would say: "Its meaning is worship of Allah. I worship Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; I humble myself to Him through hearing and obedience and by what He has commanded me."

As for His saying: ﴿the Lord of this House﴾, it refers to the honoured Ka'bah, and Allah the Exalted has attributed it to Himself in His saying: ﴿And purify My House for those who circumambulate, stand, bow and prostrate﴾ [al-Hajj 26]. Here He attributed its lordship to Himself, saying: ﴿the Lord of this House﴾.

Is He the Lord of other things too? The answer: Yes, but the attribution of lordship to Him here is by way of honour and glorification.

Now, ﴿My House﴾ — is not everything Allah's? To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth; everything belongs to Allah, everything is Allah's possession. Why then did Allah attribute the House to Himself? For honour and glorification.

So He specified it with lordship, that is, He specified the House with lordship once, and attributed it to Himself another time, for honour and glorification.

In another verse: ﴿I have only been commanded to worship the Lord of this city, which He has made sacred﴾, and after it, what did He say? ﴿And to Him belongs everything﴾ [an-Naml 91], as a safeguard lest some deluded person imagine that He is the Lord of the city alone; so He said: ﴿And to Him belongs everything﴾. Each context has a fitting expression. In His saying: ﴿I have only been commanded to worship the Lord of this city, which He has made sacred﴾ there is a context requiring the explanation of the generality of His dominion, lest the polytheists claim that He is only the Lord of the city; but here the context is one of glorifying the House, so mentioning it alone was appropriate.

﴿Who has fed them against hunger and made them safe from fear﴾. ﴿Who﴾ (الذي): is this an adjective of ﴿Lord﴾ or of ﴿House﴾?

* Students: Of ﴿Lord﴾.

* The Shaykh: Of ﴿Lord﴾. So its position is in the accusative case (نصب), and for this reason it is good to pause and say: ﴿So let them worship the Lord of this House﴾, then say: ﴿who has fed them﴾; because if you connected and said: ﴿the Lord of this House (3) who has fed them﴾, the listener would think that ﴿who﴾ is an adjective of ﴿House﴾, and this is far from the meaning and the meaning would not stand.

﴿Who has fed them against hunger and made them safe from fear﴾: Allah the Exalted explained His blessing upon them, both the apparent and the hidden blessing. Feeding them against hunger is a protection from perishing in a hidden matter, which is the food they eat; and ﴿made them safe from fear﴾ is a protection from disagreement in the matter — what? — the apparent; because fear is apparent. When the lands are surrounded by enemies, their people fear and refrain from going out and remain in their shelters. So Allah reminded them of this blessing: ﴿He fed them against hunger and made them safe from fear﴾. The safest place on earth is Makkah; it is the safest place on earth, and therefore its trees are not cut, its grass is not uprooted, its fallen things are not picked up except by one who will announce them, its game is not hunted, and blood is not shed in it. These characteristics are not found in other lands. Even Madinah is sacred and has a sanctuary (haram), but its sanctuary is far below the sanctuary of Makkah. The sanctuary of Makkah: no Muslim can enter it who has not entered it for the first time except in ihram; he is obliged to enter in ihram. Madinah is not like that. The sanctuary of Makkah makes its grass and trees forbidden absolutely, whereas for the sanctuary of Madinah some of its trees are permitted for cultivation and the like. The game of Makkah is forbidden and there is a penalty for it; the game of Madinah carries no penalty. The main point is that the greatest safe place is Makkah; even the trees are safe in it, and even the game is safe in it. Were it not that Allah made things easy for His servants, even the livestock — I mean the cattle that are not game — would be... but Allah has had mercy on the servants and permitted them to slaughter and sacrifice in this place. This blessing Allah reminded them of in His saying: ﴿Have they not seen that We made a sacred sanctuary secure, while people are snatched away from around them?﴾ [al-'Ankabut 67]; meaning: will they not thank Allah for this? So this surah, as you see, is entirely a reminder to the Quraysh of what Allah has bestowed upon them in this great House, in security from fear, and in feeding from hunger.

If someone says: What is the duty of the Quraysh regarding this blessing? And likewise, what is the duty of whoever dwells in Makkah now, of the Quraysh or others?

We say: The duty is gratitude to Allah the Exalted by performing His obedience, carrying out His command and avoiding His prohibitions. For this reason, when sins increase in the sanctuary, the danger to its people is greater than the danger to others, because sin in a noble place is greater than sin in a less noble place. This is why Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And whoever intends therein deviation by wrongdoing — We will make him taste a painful punishment﴾ [al-Hajj 25]. Allah threatened whoever intends within it — that is, whoever resolves within it upon deviation — let alone one who actually commits deviation.

It is obligatory upon a person to remember Allah's blessing upon him in every place, not only in Makkah. Our country, praise be to Allah, is today among the safest countries of the world, and among the most abundant and comfortable of the world's countries in livelihood. Allah has fed us against hunger and made us safe from fear. So it is incumbent upon us to thank Allah for this blessing, to cooperate in righteousness and piety, in enjoining good and forbidding evil, in calling to Allah upon insight, with deliberation and carefulness, and to be brothers bound together in affection.

And it is obligatory upon us — especially upon students of knowledge — when they differ among themselves, to sit together for consultation and calm discussion aimed at reaching the truth. Whenever the truth becomes clear to a person, it is obligatory upon him to follow it, and it is not permissible for him to defend his opinion, because he is not an infallible lawgiver who says: "My opinion is the correct one and whatever else is wrong." The obligation upon the believing person is to be as Allah wants him to be: ﴿It is not for a believing man or a believing woman, when Allah and His Messenger have decreed a matter, that they should have any choice about their affair. And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger has certainly strayed into clear error﴾ [al-Ahzab 36]. As for a person defending his opinion and insisting upon what he is on even when it has become clear to him that it is false, this is an error; this is the habit of the polytheists who refused to follow the Messenger and said: ﴿Indeed, we found our fathers upon a religion, and indeed we are following in their footsteps, guided﴾ [az-Zukhruf 22].

We ask Allah to perpetuate for us and for you the blessing of Islam and security in our homelands, and to make us brothers bound together upon the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him and upon his family.
